property_summary: For any caller address, only the current owner can successfully call setOwner (so after any call setOwner either leaves owner unchanged or was called by the current owner and owner becomes the provided new owner); the mutant that compares msg.sender to tx.origin instead allows non-owner EOAs calling via contracts and thus can change owner when a contract calls setOwner, violating this rule.

For any caller (including contracts), only the current owner may successfully change owner via setOwner; the mutant that uses tx.origin instead of owner allows a contract (whose msg.sender != tx.origin) to change owner, violating this invariant for some contract-caller input.

For every caller address, only the current owner can successfully call setOwner (i.e., calls to setOwner succeed iff msg.sender == c.owner()); the mutant that compares msg.sender to tx.origin allows a contract caller (msg.sender != tx.origin) to be accepted when it is not the owner, so a contract-mediated call can change owner and break this rule.

For all callers (EOA or contract) and target owner addresses, only the current owner (as stored in c.owner()) can successfully change owner via setOwner; the mutant using tx.origin allows a malicious contract (acting with tx.origin set to an EOA different from the current owner) to change owner, violating this invariant for some contract-caller input.

For any callee address X and newOwner Y, any direct call to setOwner made by X succeeds (does not revert) iff X equals the current on-chain owner; the mutant that uses tx.origin instead of owner can be bypassed by a contract caller and thus allows owner to be changed by a non-owner contract, violating this property for some contract caller input.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) returns true and updates the public owner to x; the mutant returns true but does not update owner for some inputs (owner-changing calls), so the rule is broken.
